The former name: between Phase 1 and Phase 8 of the TREE-COMMITS-SAVE campaign `codkit sync` was a usage error without an envelope (exit 2, "renamed to codkit load"), so that scripts carrying the old meaning would break loudly; since Phase 8 the name belongs to the two-way command - `##CMD-SYNC-TWO-WAY` above. @status:spec/done

**The extension of `--discard` (decision D-S3-5, confirmed by the owner on 2026-09-08, option 2):** only together with `--fresh` does the `--discard` flag drop, besides tree commits, the working-tree edits of **tracked upstream files without marker blocks** (today `CK-E-DIRTY-TREE`, a manual `git checkout` in the managed tree): the plan prints every such path as a `discard <path>` line before the first write, the actual discarding matches the plan one for one (R14), and the file returns to the pin plus the delta. Never discarded: files with marker blocks (an unextracted intervention may live there - `save` is for it; such a file stays a `CK-E-DIRTY-TREE` refusal even with `--discard`), own code and own extensions (their side of the truth is `save`/`load` per PROP-008), and untracked files outside the cleanup lists. Without `--fresh` the `--discard` flag still touches tree commits only. The reason: a build of the tree rewrites a tracked file with a build artifact that is byte-for-byte indistinguishable from a human edit, and returning to dev mode must not require a git command typed by hand in a managed tree. Rejected: a separate flag (a second name for the same "sacrifice by name" gesture), and a list of the known side effects of a build (it cannot be kept current across pins). The norm of the release protocol: packaging preferably runs in a throwaway clone, as `publish` does, so that the dev tree receives no build artifacts. @status:spec/done

`codkit load [--inputs working|pinned] [--no-inputs]` delivers the inputs of the configuration (`##INPUTS`) into the tree after the delta, on the fast path as well: the branch cannot vouch for files it does not carry. By default each input is taken from the **working tree** of its repository, uncommitted edits included (`##INPUTS-SOURCE`), so the tree shows the current content next to the current code; `--inputs pinned` takes the pinned commits instead, the way `ci` and `publish` do; `--no-inputs` builds and delivers none and leaves what the tree carries as it is, for an offline or a fast iteration. A value of `--inputs` other than `working` or `pinned`, and `--inputs` together with `--no-inputs`, is exit 2 `CK-E-CONFIG` before anything is read. The builds run after the drift guard and before the first write of the run, so a refusal of `##INPUTS-BUILD` (exit 2) leaves the tree as it was; `--fresh` builds every input again whatever its stamp; `--dry-run` builds and delivers none and says so. `data.inputs` is `[{name, to, mode, commit, files, written, removed, built}]` - `commit` is null for a working tree, `built` is false when the stamp (PROP-006 `INPUTS-STAMP`) let the run reuse the last build - and each input prints one line: `input <name>: <the working tree|commit12> -> <to>: N file(s), W written, R removed (built|unchanged since the last build)`. `--inputs` of `load` selects the source of the inputs, while `package --inputs <dir>` names the directory of the downloads of a packaging run: one spelling on two commands, with two meanings. @status:impl/done
6. codkit status

Print: the pin; the tip of the branch; tree commits outside patchset - the line `tree commits not in patchset: N` plus up to 20 `<short> <subject>` lines (`data.treeCommits: {base, count, commits}`); with N>0 the `reload needed …` line is NOT printed - moving to patchset is exactly what would destroy those commits, and the question is addressed to `save`; the currency of the branch (up to date / reload needed) is printed when N=0; **the line `loaded from patchset commit: <sha|dirty|none|unknown>`** and, when the delta has shifted away from the mark, **`patchset moved since load: N artifact(s)`** with the list (the data of the manual `CK-E-PATCHSET-MOVED` recipe; `data.loadedFrom`, `data.patchsetMoved`; the TREE-COMMITS-SAVE campaign, decision D10, Phase 7); own code - N changed files (the tree against `delta/own/`); own extensions - the line `own extensions: D declared, P path(s) differ between tree and patchset` with the list (PROP-005 `OWN-EXTENSION-UNIT`; `data.ownExtensions: {declared, differing}`), and their `extensions/<name>/` directories in the tree are own, not upstream dirt; **a stranded materialization** - an untracked `extensions/<name>/` directory of the tree that no declaration covers and that does not exist on the pin (the declaration was withdrawn, and a `load` without `--fresh` does not touch the directory - PROP-005 `OWN-EXTENSION-STRANDED`): the line `own extensions: … , S stranded materialization(s)` with the list of paths and the hint `codkit load --fresh removes it`; `data.ownExtensions.stranded: [path…]`; exit code 1 (there is something to remove); upstream files - M changed (dirt against HEAD, outside the own directory and outside the declared extensions), K marker blocks in them, the validity of the markers (pairing/id); uncommitted `delta/` changes in patchset while the tree is clean (a divergence in the direction of truth). Read-only; it works even while the lock is held. Codes: 0 clean/consistent; 1 there is something unextracted (edits, own code or tree commits) or the markers are invalid (an informational command - code 1 makes it usable in scripts). Time: seconds on a full tree. @status:spec/done

**The next step `status` prints follows the layer that owns the changed file, not the count of changed files.** A tree whose only difference from the pin is a **materialized overlay target** was told to `run codkit save`, which is wrong twice: `save` is about patch targets and an overlay target is not one, and the tool already knows the right recipe and prints it elsewhere (`load --fresh`, `spec://codkit/modules/codkit/PROP-005#OVERLAY-KNOWN-MATERIALIZATION`). `status` therefore classifies its changed upstream files the way the drift guard of `load --fresh` does - bytes exactly equal to the strict composition of the configured overlays over the clean pin file are codkit's own packaging state - reports them in `data.upstream.materializedOverlayTargets`, and when they are the ONLY thing the tree carries, names them and sends the reader to `codkit load --fresh`, saying which commands leave that state behind (`overlay apply`, `codkit package --keep-overlay`). One real edit beside them brings the `save` advice back: the recipe is only right while nothing else is there. The classification is read-only and never fatal - an unreadable pin or a broken overlay artifact costs the hint and nothing else - and the exit code is unchanged: there is still something to do, so it is still 1. Measured on 2026-09-09 by a consumer reading a colleague's log. **The second layer with a recipe of its own is the packaging residue**: a changed upstream file matching `build.packageScratch` of the type is not somebody's work either but a file the packager rewrote in passing, and `save` would carry a bumped version or a build flag into the delta. Such files are reported in `data.upstream.packagingScratch`, and while they are all the tree carries the line names them and sends the reader to `codkit load --fresh --discard` - the discard, because those bytes are a real edit of a tracked file and nothing else gives them up - adds that `codkit package` returns them itself unless the run was interrupted, and still names `save` for the reader who wrote the file themselves (`spec://codkit/modules/codkit/PROP-016#TYPE-PACKAGE-SCRATCH`). @status:spec/done

`status` reports the inputs after the own extensions: `inputs: N declared`, then one line per input - `<name> -> <to>: N file(s) from <the working tree|commit12>` or `not delivered yet`, with `, K path(s) edited in the fork tree` and one line per such path (`edited|added|removed <to>/<path> - belongs to <repository>; codkit load puts the input back`). For the repository of each input it warns when the pin is behind HEAD (`input <name>: the pin <ref12> is N commit(s) behind HEAD <head12> of its repository; codkit inputs pin <name> moves it`), when the pin is not an ancestor of HEAD or not a commit of the repository, when its working tree has changes of its own (`… has N uncommitted change(s); the pin does not carry them`) and when the repository is not there - so nobody releases other content than the tree shows without being told. A location `codkit.local.json` gives for a name `codkit.json` does not declare is named too. An edited path raises the exit code to 1, as unextracted work does, with its recipe beside it, which is never `save`; a stale pin and a repository with changes do not. `data.inputs` is `[{name, to, repository, ref, delivered: {mode, commit, files}|null, edits: [{path, kind}], repositoryState: {present, head, pin, behind, uncommitted}}]`, `pin` being `at-head`, `behind`, `diverged`, `missing-commit` or null without a HEAD. @status:impl/done
7. codkit save [path…] [--commit] [--message m] [--squash] [--allow-new-file path]

Extract the work (the algorithm is PROP-008 §4). Without arguments it takes every changed file; with paths it is targeted. Work = the resulting state of the tree relative to the last applied tip - committed and uncommitted together, tree commits included (PROP-008 §4 `##SAVE-CONSUMES-TREE-COMMITS`). **Tree commits are replayed one by one by default** (PROP-008 §4 `##SAVE-REPLAYS-TREE-COMMITS`): every foreign commit becomes a separate patchset commit with the original message, author and date plus the trailer `Codkit-Tree-Commit: <sha40>`; the person running the command commits, with their own identity. The analogy of the merge buttons of a pull request: the default is "rebase and merge", `--squash` is "squash and merge" (one commit `codkit save: squash of N tree commit(s)` listing `sha subject` in its body and carrying a trailer for every folded sha; `--message` supplies its subject); there is no analogue of "merge commit" by construction - the two histories live in two repositories, and there is no place for a third button. The uncommitted remainder lands in the working tree of patchset and is not committed; `--commit` commits it as a separate commit `codkit save: <N> file(s)` (`--message` is for that commit only). A state that changes no artifact is skipped with a message - a visible one, not silence. Idempotency: a patchset commit with the trailer `Codkit-Tree-Commit: <sha>` means "this state is replayed already" - a repeated `save` (after an interruption, for instance) skips it, while `--squash` plays out the rest in one commit; a `save` with no changed files AND no tree commits is a no-op (exit 0, "nothing to save"); a `--squash` with no tree commits is a no-op as well, with a message that there is nothing to fold. Steps: mirroring own code (tree→patchset), validating the edits, regenerating the patches file by file, rebuilding the branch without touching files, the report. A targeted `save <paths>` does not touch the branch while tree commits exist, and says that the commits stay until a full save (`##SAVE-SCOPED-BRANCH-RULE`). **The patchset shift** (the TREE-COMMITS-SAVE campaign, decisions D17/D18, Phase 7): before any write, `save` checks that patchset has not moved under the tree since the last load - an edited artifact or a `git switch` to another branch → exit 1 `CK-E-PATCHSET-MOVED`, nothing written (no artifact, no own byte, no commit, the ref untouched), the text carrying the sha of the load, the list of shifted artifacts and the manual recipe (PROP-008 §4 `##PATCHSET-MOVED-RULE`, `##LINEAGE-CHECK`; the recipe is in the FAQ as well); a patchset that was dirty at the moment of the load is a warning and the run continues. Codes: 0; 1 (an edit outside the markers - including one in an intermediate commit, named with the sha/subject of that commit - a forbidden target, the deletion of an upstream file, a malformed `Cause:` in the message of a tree commit, HEAD off the branch while foreign commits exist - `CK-E-TREE-HEAD` - the patchset shift - `CK-E-PATCHSET-MOVED` - with the exact files/lines and a hint); 2. @status:spec/done

Clarifications from the M0 implementation: a targeted `save <paths>` does NOT rebuild the branch while changes remain OUTSIDE the paths (a rebuild would wipe out unextracted work) - it prints a warning, and a full `save` completes the branch; a `--commit` on a delta that already matches the last commit is "nothing to commit", exit 0; an own edit on the patchset side alone extracts nothing (the next `load` delivers the patchset version). @status:impl/done

`save` extracts TWO layers: patch and own (and under `--commit` it stages only their paths). The overlay/resource/removed/rule layers are authored by hand on the patchset side and committed with ordinary commits; `load` delivers them into the tree (materialization). The lesson of the M1 polygon: editing a resource target in the tree leads `save` to an honest `CK-E-HEADER-MISSING` (the file changed, there is no patch) - the resource procedure is to place the artifact in `delta/resources/` by hand and then run `load`. The defect "the first `save` after a hand-written resource artifact tripped over its own guard" is FIXED in M1: the guard "nothing must move" tolerates overwrites explained by artifacts of the non-patch layers of the materializable plan (they are printed as info), and it still raises `CK-E-INTERNAL` on unexplained ones. A target described by a patch and by a resource at once falls among the "explained" ones - that is an authoring error of the delta (two artifacts for one file), and it has no guard of its own. @status:impl/done

`save` takes nothing from the directory of an input (`##INPUTS-EDITS`): an edit found there against what codkit delivered, or a path the command line names inside one, is exit 1 `CK-E-DIRTY-TREE` before anything is written, with one line per path (`edited|added|removed <to>/<path> (input <name>)`) and the hint naming the repositories the changes belong to; the next `load` delivers the change made there and puts the input's bytes back in the tree. @status:impl/done
8. codkit marker new file --id CK-… --type t --owner o --reason text [--category c] [--layer patch|entry-module] [--line n]

Scaffold a marker block: it inserts a pair of markers in the form that matches the file's extension at the `--line` line (or at the end of the file). Required flags: `--id`, `--type`, `--owner`, `--reason`; `--category` defaults to `follow`; `--layer` is `patch|entry-module` and defaults to `patch` (`rewrite-rule` is reserved for the rule generator and is forbidden here). The file is edited in the tree only; `save` then creates the patch. Checks: the id is unique (against the existing patches, the drafts and the blocks of the target file; once the inventory exists, against it too), and the file is an upstream one (not own, not a forbidden target). Idempotency: a repeat with the same id is a refusal, 1, "id already used". `--add-block` (see `CMD-MARKER-NEW-ADD-BLOCK`) is a second block of the same intervention in the same file. Codes (the M0 clarification): wrong usage (a flag value outside the lists of the conventions) → 2 `CK-E-CONFIG`; the state of the tree or of the delta (a forbidden target, a taken id, an unknown owner, a malformed id) → 1. @status:spec/done

`codkit marker new <file> --id <id> --add-block [--line <n>]` is one more marker block of an intervention the file already carries (PROP-004 `MR-SEVERAL-BLOCKS-ONE-ID`: a graft is an import and a call site). Conditions: the id belongs to this file - its header stands in the file's patch artifact or in its pending draft (otherwise 1 `CK-E-MARKER-DUP-ID`, "is not the intervention of"); the file already contains a block with that id (otherwise 1 `CK-E-MARKER-ARTIFACT-MISMATCH`, "carries no block … yet", with the hint `codkit load`); the header flags (`--type`, `--owner`, `--reason`, `--category`, `--layer`) are forbidden together with `--add-block` - 2 `CK-E-CONFIG`: an intervention has one header. The draft is neither written nor changed; `save` gathers every block of the id into one patch. `--json`: `data: {target, id, line, block: 'added'}`. @status:spec/done

**The header draft** (an implementation decision of M0 that closes the gap "marker new printed the header into nowhere"): `marker new` writes the header fields of the future patch into `.codkit/pending/<enc(target)>.json` (`{id,layer,type,category,owner,reason,link:"none"}`), where `layer` is always present and holds either the explicit value or the `patch` default; one target is reserved by exactly one draft or by an existing `.ckpatch`, a second `marker new` with a different id is rejected **before** the tree is changed and never overwrites the draft, while an exact repeat of the same unfinished operation idempotently completes the "marker + draft" pair; `save`, when it creates a NEW patch, takes the header from here and removes the draft; an existing patch keeps its own header byte for byte. Neither an existing patch nor a draft for a new target file → exit 1 `CK-E-HEADER-MISSING` with the hint "run codkit marker new <file> --id … first". The drafts are local (`.codkit/` is not committed) - the metadata reaches git only inside a `.ckpatch`. @status:spec/done
9. codkit reresolve file [--patch file]

A 3-way application of an old hunk onto the current tree file (scenario R1: a conflict of two branches over one patch file is resolved by a replay, `common/PROP-002` `##CONFLICT-RESOLVED-BY-REPLAY`). Precondition: an "old" patch exists. Its source is chosen as strictly the first existing option in this order: (1) the path from an explicit `--patch`; (2) the adjacent `<patch-path>.orig` left by a merge tool; (3) the blob `git show HEAD:<patch-path>` while the merge is still under way (`MERGE_HEAD` exists and `HEAD` is the feature tip before the merge); (4) the blob `git show HEAD^1:<patch-path>` from an already created two-parent merge commit whose first parent is the feature before the merge. `MERGE_HEAD` is not a source of the old feature patch. If no source exists, exit 1 with the list of the sources that were checked and a hint to pass `--patch`. The algorithm: base = the file at the pin; ours = the current file in the tree (already carrying the version of the target branch); theirs = base + the old patch; `git merge-file` (PROP-008 §5). Clean → the file in the tree is updated and it prints "resolved, run codkit save"; a conflict → the standard conflict markers are left in the tree file, exit 1, hint "edit conflicts in IDE, then codkit save". @status:spec/done
10. codkit inventory [--diff ref] [--md]

Generate the inventory (PROP-006 §3–4) into `.codkit/out/inventory.json` (and `.md` under `--md`); print a summary of the metrics. `--diff <ref>`: build the inventory for the patchset state at `<ref>` as well (reading the artifacts through `git show <ref>:<path>` without a checkout) and print the diff: added/removed/changed entries plus the delta of the metrics; the format is a table by id. Codes: 0; 1 - the inventory was built, but there are consistency violations (the same checks `verify` makes, in reporting mode); 2. @status:spec/done

`inventory` prints the inputs after its summary - `N input(s) from other repositories:` and one `<name> <ref12> -> <to>` line each - and puts them into `data.inputs` as `[{name, ref, from, to}]`. The inventory document does not carry them: it lists the interventions of the delta (PROP-006 `INVENTORY-IS-GENERATED`), and an input is none; a new pin of an input is a change of `codkit.json`, which the review reads. @status:impl/done
11. codkit verify

Every integrity check without a build (the PR threshold; seconds): the markers are valid; every hunk of every patch is inside the markers; the "marker ↔ artifact" consistency holds in both directions; the ids are unique; the owner exists; the config-overlay/resource-file layers and the hide category have a guard test; for rules, `expectedMatches` agrees; for overlays, `expectUpstream` agrees; own files are covered by units; the removed registry is covered by guard tests; "there are no interventions outside the inventory"; `forbiddenServiceIds` do not overlap. It requires the tree (for the checks against the pin it uses the git objects of the tree and does not read the working files - it works on a dirty tree as well). Codes: 0; 1 (any violation; each on a line of its own, `code: file:line: text + hint`); 2. @status:spec/done
12. codkit overlay new|apply|check file

`check`: for an overlay target - schema validation, `expectUpstream` against the pin, and (when the target is materialized in the tree) the comparison "the current content = the pin + the operations". `apply`: materialization by option 2 (PROP-005 §5) - overwriting the target file in the tree. An ordinary developer does not need it (`load` covers the dev channel); packaging, `publish` and `ci` use it. Codes: 0; 1 (`CK-E-OVERLAY-DRIFT` - apply refuses on drift as well: an intervention whose upstream expectation is broken must not be materialized); 2. A note (M1, REPAIR-005): `overlay apply` on a developer's tree makes the next ordinary `load` red with `CK-E-DIRTY-TREE` - which is right by the model (apply is a packaging operation; an ordinary `load` cannot withdraw its own bytes silently: the fast path would answer "up to date" and leave the packaging bytes standing). The way back to dev mode is `codkit load --fresh`: before refusing, the guard classifies every tracked overlay target that differs from HEAD, and only bytes exactly equal to the strict composition of the configured overlays count as a known codkit materialization that the run replaces (PROP-005 §5 `##OVERLAY-KNOWN-MATERIALIZATION`); any extra, missing or hand-made byte stays dirt. A direct `git checkout` of the target is not needed. @status:spec/done

**What `check` calls a materialized target** - the tree side of `##CMD-OVERLAY`, which compares the file with "the pin + the operations" only when the target is materialized. The target counts as materialized when its **content** differs from the pin's blob, and the content of a file is what git stores for it at its path: git's own hash of the file under the tree's attributes (`git hash-object -- <target>` in codkit's isolated configuration, PROP-002 `##GIT-ENV-ISOLATION`), not its raw bytes. A file that differs from the pin's blob only by git's working-copy conversion is the pin's file, because git itself calls it unchanged: the CRLF line endings a checkout on Windows writes for a `text=auto` file of upstream - which is what a `git checkout -- <target>` there leaves behind - are not an edit. On such a tree, and on one that has no such file at all, the target is **not materialized**: `check` does not compare it with the operations and does not report `CK-E-OVERLAY-DRIFT` over it; it says so in its own line (`<target>: N overlay(s) agree with the pin; the target is not materialized in the fork tree …`) and in its own status, `data.inTree: "pin"` or `"absent"` with `matchesOperations: null`, and exits 0. The codes of `##CMD-OVERLAY` stay 0, 1 and 2: a target that is not materialized is a check that passed, and it is the everyday state of a development tree, whose `product.json` stays the pin's while `load` writes the dev channel. A materialized target (`data.inTree: "materialized"`, `materialized: true`) is compared byte for byte with the strict composition of PROP-005 `##OVERLAY-KNOWN-MATERIALIZATION`: equal bytes are `matchesOperations: true` and exit 0; any other bytes - a hand edit of the pin's file or of a materialization, a stale materialization, a converted copy of one - are `CK-E-OVERLAY-DRIFT`, exit 1, `matchesOperations: false`. `apply` reports the same three fields for the file as it found it. @status:impl/done

`codkit overlay new <target> --id CK-… --type t --owner o --reason text [--category c] --contract-test <id>…` scaffolds the artifact of this layer, the way `marker new` scaffolds a patch and `gen feature` an own unit. It exists because writing one by hand was a refusal by construction: the metadata has to be canonical JSON in the **schema's key order**, and `CK-E-ARTIFACT-BROKEN: metadata bytes are not canonical JSON` names the rules - key order, two-space indentation, UTF-8 without BOM, LF, one final LF - without naming the order, which lives in the serializer. Every first overlay of every patch set therefore cost one refusal that taught nothing. The command writes `delta/overlays/<target with / as __>.overlay.json`: the canonical metadata, the pin of `codkit.json` as `<tag>@<sha>`, `link` and `cause` as the literal `none`, the guard tests of `--contract-test`, and an **empty** list of operations for the author to fill in. `--contract-test` is repeatable and required - a guard test is mandatory for this layer (PROP-005 §5), because the overlay leaves no marker in the target file and the test is the only thing that fails when upstream takes the key away - and there is no `--layer`: the artifact IS the layer. The metadata is held to the same vocabularies `marker new` holds an intervention to (the id pattern, the intervention types, the categories, an owner of `delta/owners.json`), the id must be free among the overlays of the delta, and an existing artifact of the target is never overwritten. A target the project type does not declare is a warning and not a refusal - the layer already restricts an undeclared target to the strictest keys the type states (PROP-005 `##OVERLAY-NON-PRODUCT-TARGETS`) - and no fork tree is touched or needed: the target is a path in the tree, not a file this command reads. Codes: 0; 1 - the state of the delta (`CK-E-MARKER-BAD-ID`, `CK-E-MARKER-DUP-ID`, `CK-E-OWNER-UNKNOWN`, `CK-E-GEN-EXISTS`); 2 - what was typed or the configuration (`CK-E-CONFIG`). `--json`: `data: {artifact, target, id, type, category, owner, reason, pin, contractTests, operations: 0}`. @status:spec/done
13. codkit build up|down|status|errors [--channel c] [--mine] [--timeout s]

A wrapper over the watch daemons (PROP-010 §2). Channels: `transpile`, `typecheck`, `extensions`, `copilot` for the `vscode` type, `typecheck` and `bundle` for `theia`, whatever the patch set declared for `generic`; `--channel all` is all of them. **The default of `up` - and of the one pass of `ci --profile build` - is the type's own answer** (`build.defaultChannels`, `spec://codkit/modules/codkit/PROP-016#TYPE-BUILD-CHANNELS`) and not a pair of names the engine carries: the pair `transpile,typecheck` was a module constant until a family whose channels are `typecheck` and `bundle` met it, and that family's build profile therefore never bundled its application. A name the profile does not declare is ignored, and a type that names none has every declared channel as its default, so the bare form of the command is never a refusal over a name from another family (clarified on 2026-09-09 with the `theia` type, corrected the same day when the constant was found in the ci engine as well). `up` starts the missing daemons in the background (detached, logs in `.codkit/build/<channel>.log`) and does not wait for the end of a pass; `down` stops them (by the process tree); `status` reports living/dead per channel (by probing the command line of the process, not by a pid file); `errors` waits for the end of the current pass and prints the errors of the last finished pass in full (`--mine` narrows it to files from the inventory and own code). The rule (in our own words from the clean-room rewriting): running the compiler over the whole project directly is forbidden - the daemons carry the compilation; `errors` is called once and its output is read in full. The codes of `errors`: 0 there are no errors; 1 there are errors; 2 the daemon is not running AND there is no finished pass in the log (hint "codkit build up"); a dead daemon with a FINISHED pass in the log gives the result of that pass (0/1) plus a warning (useful for a single CI pass; the M1 clarification). The bounds of the post-mortem view (the M1 implementation): a pass from the log is given out only when a daemon record EXISTS (the record ties the log to a particular start and a particular tree; `up` rotates the log exactly when it creates the record) - a channel without a record was either never started or was stopped by `build down`, which retires the channel together with its answer; the LAST FINISHED pass is what is given out (a daemon that died inside a new pass gives out the previous finished one); without `--channel` the channels that have an answer are listed (the living ones and the dead ones with a pass). The codes of the other subcommands (the M1 clarification): `up` - 0 started or already living, 1 a refusal (a foreign watcher, no script, a channel of another tree, a concurrent start), 2 the tree is unfit; `down`/`status` - always 0. The spelling of "all channels" is `--channel all` (one single form). Dedicated `CK-E-*` codes for these refusals are deliberately not created until their machine consumer (the skill of the cycle, M2) appears. @status:spec/done

REPAIR-009 clarifies the semantics without changing the codes: `build status` stays report-only and its exit 0 means that the OBSERVATION succeeded, not that every daemon is healthy - `starting` and `unknown` stay visible states in the line and in the JSON, and this is said explicitly in the reference and JSON documentation. `up` and `down` hold a contained per-channel operation lock (PROP-010 ##DAEMON-CHANNEL-LOCK) from the first probe to the final publication or the exact retirement; a competitor that loses returns a refusal without touching either the record or the process. `status`, `down` and `errors` are bound to the current tree: a record of another tree is shown honestly, `down` sends no signals, `errors` does not certify a foreign log, and a mutating or certifying mismatch is an environment code. @status:impl/done
14. codkit cycle start tag|sha / continue / status / restart [--yes] [--ci]

The orchestrator of the upgrade (PROP-009). `start` - preconditions: there is no active cycle (no `cycle/state.json`), the working tree of patchset is clean, and the target pin is reachable in the tree (otherwise 2 with a hint saying which fetch to run - there is no network); it creates the cycle branch and the pin commit, and starts the apply phase. `continue` - after a manual or agent resolution: it re-reads the state, extracts the resolutions that remain (a `save` of the affected files) and carries on through the phases. `status` - print the phase, the outcome counters and `nextAction`. `restart` - a reset to the beginning of the cycle: `git reset --hard` of the cycle branch to the parent of the pin commit plus the removal of `cycle/state.json` (confirmed by the `--yes` flag; under `--ci` only with `--yes`). `--ci` is the non-interactive keep-alive mode: the stopping points do not wait but end the process with code 3 and a full report. Codes: 0 the phase or the cycle is finished; 1 checks; 2 the environment; 3 a stop for a human. @status:spec/done
15. codkit forecast [--ref upstream-ref]

A dry run of applying the delta onto an upstream ref. The choice is deterministic: the explicit `--ref <ref>`, otherwise exactly `refs/remotes/upstream/main`; searching for "the freshest" among similar refs, and a fallback to `origin/main`, are forbidden. The chosen name is resolved once through `git rev-parse --verify '<ref>^{commit}'` into a full SHA, and that SHA is printed and used by the whole run; a missing ref → exit 2 with a hint to pass `--ref` or to update the mirror beforehand. Under the global `--ci` the `--ref` flag is required, and its absence → exit 2 before the tree is read or changed. The implementation: the same apply engine in dry-run mode against the resolved SHA instead of the pin. The output is a report by owner: for every artifact whose outcome is worse than `clean` - the id, the owner, the outcome and the cause. There is no network: the freshness of the ref is the duty of CI (the mirror bot). Codes: 0 everything is clean; 1 there are future breakages (the "informational redness" of a nightly job); 2. @status:spec/done
16. codkit rebase-onto-pin

Rebinding the patches of a patchset feature branch to the pin of the target branch after an ordinary merge (guard R2b). The command does not guess `main` by name and does not use the merged `HEAD` as a source of feature patches. @status:spec/done

`HEAD` must be a merge commit with exactly two parents: `HEAD^1` is the feature tip before the merge, `HEAD^2` is the merged-in target branch. A non-merge, an octopus merge, an unfinished merge and swapped parent roles are rejected with code 2 and a hint to repeat `git merge <target>` on the feature branch. The target pin is taken only from `codkit.json` at `HEAD^2`; the pin in the merged `HEAD` must match it. The source pin is taken from `codkit.json` at `HEAD^1`; both full SHAs must be reachable in the tree. @status:spec/done

`M = git merge-base HEAD^1 HEAD^2` is computed. The transferable set is the `delta/patches/*.ckpatch` files existing at `HEAD^1` whose paths appear in `git diff --name-status M..HEAD^1 -- delta/patches/`; the blob of every patch is read strictly from `HEAD^1`. Feature deletions and renames are already resolved by the merge itself and are taken from the merged working state; patches changed by the target branch alone are not part of the transfer. @status:spec/done

The target baseline is built in a scratch index and scratch objects from the patchset state at `HEAD^2`: its delta is applied onto its target pin, without the feature patches of the transferable set. Checking out a patchset ref, changing the refs of the tree and using already merged blobs for the baseline are forbidden. The feature patches from `HEAD^1` are applied onto that baseline one by one through PROP-008 §5; only after the full classification is the result carried into the working tree. @status:spec/done

For `clean|shifted|merged|target-renamed` the patch is regenerated as the state "the target pin → the transferred file": every other header field is preserved, and `pin` becomes the exact `<tag>@<sha>` from `HEAD^2`. The old `cause` is preserved only for `clean` without a rename; for `shifted|merged|conflict|target-renamed|target-deleted` the cause of the change between the source and the target pin is computed per PROP-008 §7 (including `approx`; for `target-deleted` it stays in the red report until a human decides). For a conflict the target `pin/cause` are held in the local pending context of the operation and are written into the `.ckpatch` only together with the new body, by a subsequent `codkit save`; the intermediate pair "a new pin + an old body" is never written. @status:spec/done

Conflicts are materialized with the standard markers in the tree files over the scratch baseline of the target branch, and they are listed in full; after a manual resolution `codkit save` is run, and it finishes the pending regeneration. Codes: 0 - everything transferred cleanly; 1 - there are conflicts or broken feature artifacts; 2 - the merge or environment contract is violated. @status:spec/done
17. codkit ci [--profile verify|build] [--effective-diff base-ref]

The container run "from scratch" (PROP-011). It always implies `--ci` (zero network). Profiles: `verify` (the default) - identity → a fresh bring-up to the pin → the apply → `verify` plus the race guards; `build` - the same plus the dependencies (the fast path), one compilation pass through the daemons, own tests and contract tests. Codes: 0; 1; 2. @status:spec/done

The implementation after the post-M1 audit. The full signature: `ci [--profile verify|build] [--effective-diff <base-ref>] [--pin-guard-base <ref>] [--timeout <sec>]`; the command holds a per-tree lock for the whole run. The steps of verify (7 of them, printed in order with progress): the source of the path → the safe.directory probe (PROP-011 §5) → check-tree (in write mode) → a fresh load with the overlay targets materialized into the branch → verify → pin-guard (only with `--pin-guard-base`; otherwise the step is explicitly skipped) → effective-diff (only with the flag). Build runs 12 steps: the source → safe.directory → check-tree → a fresh load **without** the overlay targets → the dependencies → the real `npm run hygiene` and `npm run eslint` over the unmaterialized overlay → a second fresh load with overlay apply → verify → pin-guard → effective-diff → one pass of the daemons the type names (`build.defaultChannels`) → the real product/contract tests through `npm run test-node -- --runGlob vs/<ownDirName>/**/test/{common,node}/**/*.test.js` (the `common` and `node` layers of every `test/` directory under the own directory: the tests of the product, of the delivered library and of the feature directories; `--runGlob` goes around the standard exclusion of those layers by the node runner, while the suites of the `browser` layer run under the electron runner outside `ci` - PROP-010 §4). A red hygiene or test ends the command with code 1; a missing runner or script is code 2 `CK-E-LOG-INCOMPLETE`; there are no stubs that exit 0. The daemons are stopped in a finally block; an unfinished pass is `CK-E-LOG-INCOMPLETE`. Codes: 0; 1 - the checks, pin-guard, compilation or tests; 2 - the environment (`NET-FORBIDDEN`, `DEPS-MISSING`, a missing required runner). The step order is universal; the named scripts and globs are the project type's answer (VS Code type: `spec://codkit/modules/vscode/PROP-004#VSCODE-BUILD-STEPS`). @status:impl/done

`ci` takes every input from its pinned commit (`##INPUTS-SOURCE`), in both profiles and never from a working tree: a generated branch ends with one commit per input (`##INPUTS-GENERATED`), and a pass that builds no generated branch delivers them untracked as `load --inputs pinned` does. The repository of each input must be at its location on the machine that runs the job - `ci` fetches nothing (`##INPUTS-LOCAL-REPOSITORY`) - so a job provides the input repositories the way it provides the fork tree, and names their location in `codkit.local.json` when it differs from `codkit.json`. The effective diff leaves the directories of the inputs out (`-- . ':(exclude,literal)<to>'`, the `to` of the configuration and of the base): the base tip is built without them, and an input is reviewed in its own repository. @status:impl/done

18. codkit publish patchset-ref [--profile verify|build] [--release semver] [--branch name] [--squash [--orphan] --author "Name <email>" --message-file path [--scrub]] [--no-lfs] [--export-bare dir | --export-repo dir] --yes-i-am-publish-bot

Build the generated branch from an immutable patchset commit and publish it into the fork, or into a new local repository. `patchset-ref` is required and is resolved once into a full commit SHA; `--profile verify|build` selects the checks and defaults to `verify`; `--release <semver>` additionally creates a release tag. The command requires an explicit `--yes-i-am-publish-bot`, and a configured `publishRemoteUrl` unless the release goes into a new local repository (`##PUBLISH-EXPORT`); this is neither a human mode nor `--ci`: a `--ci` that is passed is rejected with code 2 `CK-E-NET-FORBIDDEN`, because publish has to reach the network - and so is a `--ci` given with an export, which reaches none, because an export is the release bot's operation as well. `--branch`, `--squash` and `--scrub` turn the release branch into a clean branch of the product source (`##PUBLISH-BRANCH-NAME`, `##PUBLISH-SQUASH`, `##PUBLISH-SCRUB`); `--squash` and `--orphan` choose the form of its history (`##PUBLISH-FORMS`, `##PUBLISH-ORPHAN`); `--no-lfs` leaves out what git-lfs tracks (`##PUBLISH-NO-LFS`); `--export-bare <dir>` and `--export-repo <dir>` write the release into a new bare repository or into a new repository with a working tree instead of `publishRemoteUrl` (`##PUBLISH-EXPORT`, `##PUBLISH-EXPORT-LFS`). The inputs of the patch set enter the release from their pinned commits (`##PUBLISH-INPUTS`). @status:spec/done

Before the fresh materialization and before any local or remote mutation, `git ls-remote <publishRemoteUrl>` is run; a failure → exit 2 naming the exact access required, with the tree and the refs unchanged. Only after the gate succeeds are the build and the push allowed; `publish` is the one codkit command where `netAllowed=true`, and only under the bot flag. An export into a new local repository (`##PUBLISH-EXPORT`) has no remote: `publishRemoteUrl` is neither required nor read, the gate is not run, nothing is pushed and no network is reached - the one git call of the run that `netAllowed` covers is the `git clone --shared` of the local fork tree into the disposable fork (`##PUBLISH-DISPOSABLE-FORK`). @status:spec/done

The history is built and checked in a disposable fork, never in the caller's tree: the resolved patchset commit is checked out into a temporary snapshot, and the fork tree is cloned with `git clone --shared --no-checkout` into a temporary directory that the run removes whatever its outcome. The fork carries in its own config what codkit's git reads from no global or system config (PROP-002 `GIT-ENV-ISOLATION`): `core.longpaths=true`, because the fork lives deeper than the tree it copies and on Windows the longest upstream paths pass the 260-character limit otherwise (a no-op elsewhere); and, when git-lfs is installed and the tree has git-lfs content, the lfs filters that `git lfs install --local --skip-repo` writes - clean, smudge, process, required, and no hooks - with `lfs.storage` naming the lfs storage of the tree's common git directory, the way `--shared` shares its objects: the checkout of the pin smudges from local content, without the network. A tree without git-lfs or without lfs content is left alone, and check-tree names what is missing. The dependency roots of the project type are copied in as they are. @status:impl/done

The history is built from the pin in `codkit.json` at the resolved `patchset-ref`, strictly in this order: (1) the patch commits one by one, lexicographically by the UTF-8 path of the `.ckpatch`; (2) one own commit for the snapshot of `delta/own/**` when the own code being delivered is non-empty - minus `LICENSE-CODKIT.md`: the release branch does not carry the Codkit notice (PROP-014 §4a `STD-NOTICE-RELEASE-EXCLUSION`); an own snapshot made of that one notice is empty, and the commit is skipped; (3) the overlay commits by target, lexicographically by target, with the overlay composition of one target; (4) the resource commits by entries sorted by target; (5) one commit per input of the configuration, in the order of its declaration, built from its pinned commit (`##INPUTS-GENERATED`). Then the selected profile of checks is run. Every one of these generated commits carries the canonical trailers with the exact case: `Codkit-Patchset-Commit: <the full 40-hex SHA of patchset-ref>` and `Codkit-Upstream-Pin: <pin.tag>@<the full 40-hex pin.sha>`. Under `--no-lfs` without `--squash` one more generated commit ends the history after the checks have passed (`##PUBLISH-NO-LFS`). @status:spec/done

Without `--branch` (`##PUBLISH-BRANCH-NAME`) the branch is named `codkit/release/<patchset12>+<pin.tag>`, where `patchset12` is exactly the first 12 lower-case hex characters of the resolved patchset SHA; the branch is pushed with `--force-with-lease`, or written into the new repository of an export (`##PUBLISH-EXPORT`). With `--release <semver>` the local test contract, pending the owner's decision of PROP-012 §5, creates the tag `patchset-v<semver>+<pin.tag>` on the published tip: the generated tip - the commit of `##PUBLISH-NO-LFS` when it ends the history - or the squashed commit under `--squash` (`##PUBLISH-SQUASH`). The tag is immutable: an absent one is published without force; one that already points at the same tip is an idempotent success; one that points at another tip is exit 1, with the tag neither moved nor deleted. An idempotent repeat after an interruption repeats only the pushes that were not delivered. Codes: 0; 1 - the checks or a conflict of the immutable tag; 2 - the network, the permissions or the environment. @status:spec/done

`--branch <name>` names the published branch, for example `nimbus/rc/1.0.0`; without it the name is the one of `##PUBLISH-REFS`. The name is the short name of a branch: `refs/heads/<name>` must pass `git check-ref-format`, and a name that starts with `-` or `refs/`, or is `HEAD`, is refused. It must not collide with the namespaces of the patch set: a name inside `generatedBranchPrefix`, `cycleBranchPrefix` or `releaseRefPrefix` - of the `codkit.json` of the published commit or of the effective configuration - or a name that is a leading directory of one of them (`codkit` against `codkit/applied/`) is refused. Every refusal is exit 2 before the network gate. The lease, the repeat and the tag of `##PUBLISH-REFS` apply to the named branch unchanged. @status:impl/done

**The three forms of a release.** The owner's order of 2026-09-30 asks for three forms of the published history, each chosen by a flag of `publish` and none by the configuration: (1) "one commit for everything" - `--squash --orphan` - a single commit without a parent whose tree is the whole product (`##PUBLISH-ORPHAN`); (2) "the commit history plus the squashed patch set" - `--squash` - the pin's history, then one commit with every change of the patch set (`##PUBLISH-SQUASH`); (3) "the commit history plus the commit history of the patch set" - neither flag - the pin's history, then the generated commits of `##PUBLISH-GENERATED-ORDER`. The third form is the history `publish` has always pushed without `--squash`: one commit per artifact and per input, written by the tool, and never a replay of the development history of the patch-set repository - that would be another feature. It cannot be scrubbed (`##PUBLISH-SCRUB` needs `--squash`) and keeps the tool's author and its trailers. Each form is published with or without the content git-lfs tracks (`##PUBLISH-NO-LFS`), into `publishRemoteUrl` or into a new local repository (`##PUBLISH-EXPORT`); `codkit.json` and `codkit.local.json` carry none of these choices. @status:impl/done

`--squash` publishes one commit instead of the generated history. Its parent is `pin.sha`, or none under `--orphan` (`##PUBLISH-ORPHAN`); its tree is exactly the tree of the tip the history of `##PUBLISH-GENERATED-ORDER` ends at - after `##PUBLISH-SCRUB` when `--scrub` is given as well, and after `##PUBLISH-NO-LFS` when `--no-lfs` is. That history is still built in the disposable fork and the selected profile of checks runs over it unchanged; only the squashed commit leaves the fork. `--author "<Name> <email>"` is the author and the committer: a UTF-8 name, Cyrillic included, without `<`, `>` or a line break, and a non-empty address without spaces. `--message-file <path>` is the message: strict UTF-8 without a byte order mark and without NUL, CRLF read as LF, blank lines cut at both ends, one final LF; a message without text is refused. Both dates are the committer date of the patchset commit, so one patchset commit, author and message always make the same commit and a repeat is `up-to-date`. The squashed commit carries no Codkit trailer: its traceability is the release tag, which names it, and the message the owner writes. `--squash` without both `--author` and `--message-file`, and either of them without `--squash`, is exit 2 before the network gate, and so is an unreadable file or a malformed author. `data.squash` is `{parent, tree, unsquashedTip, author}`, `parent` being null for a commit without a parent. @status:impl/done

`--orphan` writes the squashed commit of `##PUBLISH-SQUASH` without a parent: the first form of `##PUBLISH-FORMS`, one commit for everything (`##DECISION-PUBLISH-ORPHAN`). It is a modifier of `--squash` and needs it: `--orphan` without `--squash` is exit 2 `CK-E-CONFIG` before any gate - before the refusal of `--ci`, the bot flag and the network gate - with the hint that names `--squash`. Everything else of `##PUBLISH-SQUASH` holds: the tree after `--scrub` and after `--no-lfs` when they are given, `--author` as the author and the committer, the message of `--message-file`, both dates the committer date of the patchset commit, no Codkit trailer; so the same patchset commit, author, message and flags always make the same commit, and a repeat against a remote answers `up-to-date`. The release tag names this commit. `data.squash.parent` is null, and the info line of the squash says that the commit has no parent instead of naming the pin: `squash: <unsquashed12> -> <tip12> without a parent (tree <tree12>)`. A push of the commit carries only the objects it reaches: into an empty repository that is its tree and nothing of upstream's history - the pin is not an object of that repository afterwards. Measured on 2026-09-30 on the Nimbus replica (patchset commit `3eb29750960b`): `--squash --orphan --scrub --no-lfs --export-repo` made one commit over the tree the same run without `--orphan` made (`1cd1e4b4e779`), in 89 s with its checks; the pin is not an object of that repository, whose `.git` holds 60.4 MiB against 1,264 MiB with upstream's history. @status:impl/done

`--scrub` takes the tooling out of the release tree before the squashed commit is written; it needs `--squash` (a history that carries the markers is not clean), and alone it is exit 2. The delivered files are the regular files in which the unsquashed tip differs from the pin; nothing else is touched. In a delivered file that is strict UTF-8 the scrub removes: (a) every codkit marker line - a line that is only `<open>begin <name><close>` or `<open>end <name><close>` in any form of `markerComment` (PROP-004 §1: the shipped `// codkit:`, `/* codkit: … */`, `<!-- codkit: … -->`, `# codkit:` and the forms a conventions extension adds), where the name is an intervention id or the name of a managed block; (b) every `spec://` reference of a comment line: a parenthetical `(spec://…)` with its leading space - when it opens the text of the line, the punctuation right after it moves to the end of the previous comment line, if that line has text that does not end in punctuation already, and is dropped otherwise; a tag line whose only content is `@<tag> spec://…` (`@scope`, `@implements`, `@verifies` or any other tag); and a bare `spec://…` token, with its leading space; (c) the reference groups of `##PUBLISH-SCRUB-GROUPS`, in comment text and in the prose of Markdown files. A comment line is a line whose first non-blank characters open a comment of the file's syntax, or that continues a block comment opened that way on an earlier line; the syntax is the one of the file's form in `markerComment`: `//` and `/* */` for the `//` form, `/* */` for the CSS form, `<!-- -->` for the markup form, `#` for the hash form. Text after the close of a block comment on the same line is code. A comment line the scrub leaves without text is dropped, except a line that opens or closes a block comment, which keeps its delimiters. Code lines, binary files and files whose extension has no form are never altered: what they carry is left to `##PUBLISH-SCRUB-FAIL-CLOSED`. Every changed file is reported with its counts - marker lines, spec references, reference groups, dropped lines - and so is every excluded file, the vocabulary by source and the groups removed by rule; `data.scrub` is `{files: [{path, markers, specRefs, droppedLines, groups: {parenthetical, lead, sentence, preposition}}], excluded, leftovers, vocabulary: {interventions, documents, stems, facts, modules, configured, allowed}}`. The runtime library under the own root stays (PROP-015 `RT-PUBLISH-KEEPS-THE-RUNTIME`): it is product code under its own licence header, and a build file that names its `codkit/` directory names a path, not a marker. @status:impl/done

`--scrub` also takes out the bare references of the patch set - the ids it writes in prose without `spec://`. No naming pattern of any project is built in: the vocabulary is learned from the published commit and from the release. (1) The intervention ids: every id of the inventory of the published commit (PROP-006 `INVENTORY-IS-GENERATED`) and every name of a marker line of the delivered files; always on under `--scrub`. (2) The spec vocabulary, read from every `*.xml` file under the spec roots of the published commit, `publish.scrub.specRoots` (PROP-003 `CFG-PUBLISH-SCRUB-SPEC-ROOTS`), by default `vibevm/vibespecs`, where a vibevm project keeps its specifications - the layout Codkit already writes into for its standards (PROP-014 `STD-NOTICE-VIBE-COPIES` names the boot lane `vibevm/vibespecs/boot/` of the product). Of each document: its file stem (`FEAT-004-center-surfaces`); its document id, the longest part of the stem cut at a hyphen that the document's root title names as a word (`FEAT-004`, titled `nimbus FEAT-004: ...`); its fact ids, the names of the elements that carry `fact="true"` - which is how the spec dialect marks a fact - and the values of `id` attributes. Of every `spec://` reference in a delivered file: the last segment of its path, a stem or a short document id, and its fragment, a fact id. (3) The module names - the word of a root title before its document id (`nimbus`) and the first segment of a `spec://` path - are qualifiers only, never tokens. (4) `publish.scrub.vocabulary`: literal tokens and regular expressions the owner names for references that live elsewhere (`CFG-PUBLISH-SCRUB-VOCABULARY`). Every learned word passes `##PUBLISH-SCRUB-ID-SHAPE` first. The specmap is not a source: it is an index derived from the same documents, which a patch set need not carry - Nimbus carries none. A token matches case-sensitively where neither the character before it nor the one after it is a letter, a digit or `_`, the longest token first. A configured spec root that the published commit does not carry is a warning; an absent default root is silent. Measured on 2026-09-24 on the Nimbus replica: 156 intervention ids, 15 document ids, 15 stems, 582 fact ids and one module name. @status:impl/done

A learned word is a token only in the shape of an id: at least four characters, only letters, digits, `_`, `.` and `-`, opening and closing with a letter, a digit or `_`, with at least one upper-case letter and at least one hyphen or digit. The shape is read off the Nimbus data of 2026-09-24: every one of its 582 fact ids, 15 document ids and 156 intervention ids has an upper-case letter and a hyphen and is at least five characters long (the shortest are decisions such as `AP-D1`), while the generic words its sources yield lack one of these marks: `root`, the `id` of every root title, and the stem `WAL`. So do the names of the managed blocks a marker line may carry (`standards`, `components`, `scrape`) and the lower-case anchors and facts of codkit's own specifications (`config-valid-sample`). A project whose ids are lower case names them in `publish.scrub.vocabulary`, which the shape does not filter. @status:impl/done

The bare references are removed as whole reference groups, in comment text - the comment lines of `##PUBLISH-SCRUB` - and in the prose of Markdown files (`.md`, `.markdown`): every line outside fenced code, an HTML comment being comment text. A group is a maximal run of tokens and their qualifiers: a token in backticks; a module name directly before a token (`nimbus FEAT-010`); `intervention` or `interventions` before an intervention id; `decision` before a token; after a token, `section <n>` and `decision <id>`, whose `<id>` has the shape of `##PUBLISH-SCRUB-ID-SHAPE`; tokens joined by a comma, a semicolon, `and` or a blank. A group may continue onto the next line of the same comment paragraph or Markdown paragraph, and in Markdown prose a `spec://` reference is a token too. A group is removed in four places and only there: (1) a parenthetical that holds only the group, with the blank before it, also across lines - `(FEAT-007 CP-PROVIDERS)`, `(intervention `CK-build-002`)`, `(nimbus FEAT-010 AW-OWN-UNIT, AW-LOG)`, `(PROP-004` at the end of one line and `BU-D8)` on the next; (2) a group that opens a sentence and is followed by `:`, with the colon - `// FEAT-007 CP-PROVIDERS: a new chat` becomes `// a new chat`; (3) a sentence that is only the group, or `See`/`see` and the group - `See FEAT-005 `EP-SETTING`.`, `FEAT-006 `FR-TRIGGER`, `FR-GUARDS`.`; (4) a group after `of`, `in`, `by`, `per` or `from`, with the preposition - `the direction rule of FEAT-004 section 5b.` becomes `the direction rule.`, `Every rule of FEAT-004 section 5a that is about` becomes `Every rule that is about`. A sentence opens at the start of a paragraph or after `.`, `!` or `?` and a blank. Where something was removed, and only there, a blank before `.`, `,`, `:`, `;` or `)` goes, a double blank becomes one, a comma or a semicolon doubled across the gap becomes one, and a line whose start went gives its leading `.`, `,`, `;` or `:` to the end of the previous line of the paragraph when that line has text that does not end in punctuation, and drops it otherwise; a line left without text is dropped as `##PUBLISH-SCRUB` drops an emptied comment line. Every other occurrence stays in place for `##PUBLISH-SCRUB-FAIL-CLOSED` - prose the four places do not cover (`The owning specification is FEAT-004.`), a parenthetical with anything else in it, code and strings, data such as a JSON description, and a comment after code on the same line: code, fenced code and files that are neither commented nor Markdown are never altered. Measured on 2026-09-24 on the Nimbus replica: 125 parentheticals, 11 groups with a colon, 13 sentences and 12 groups after a preposition, in 112 files. @status:impl/done

`publish.exclude` names paths of the release tree, a file or a directory, that `--scrub` leaves out of the release: the list of the `codkit.json` of the published commit joined with the list of `codkit.local.json` (PROP-003 `CFG-PUBLISH-EXCLUDE`). A delivered file the pin does not carry is left out of the tree. An entry that names a path the pin carries is exit 2 before the network gate - an exclusion leaves out what the patch set adds and never deletes or reverts upstream's bytes; an entry that matches no delivered file is a warning. The one exception to that rule is `--no-lfs` (`##PUBLISH-NO-LFS`), the owner's decision of 2026-09-30 (`##DECISION-PUBLISH-NO-LFS`): a flag given on the run and never a value of the configuration, which removes only what git-lfs tracks; the refusal of this fact stands as it is. @status:impl/done

After the scrub and the exclusions the whole release tree is searched for `codkit:begin`, `codkit:end`, `spec://` and `vibevm` - the last one names the spec tooling, which is not part of the product - ignoring case, binary files included. Any hit stops the publish before the first remote write: exit 1, `data.status` `scrub-failed`, one `CK-E-CONFIG` error per hit naming the file and the line (a binary file has no line), and nothing is pushed. Every delivered file left in the tree is searched as well for the vocabulary of `##PUBLISH-SCRUB-VOCABULARY` - a text file line by line, a binary file as its bytes - with the matching of that fact: a line that still carries a token stops the publish the same way, and its error names the tokens; a line the first search already names is named once. The files the pin carries unchanged are upstream's bytes, never a reference of the patch set, and are not searched for vocabulary. A leftover of `data.scrub.leftovers` is `{path, line, text, tokens}`, with `tokens` empty for a hit of the first search. The way out is the owner's: an exclusion, a change of the file in the patch set, or - for a token the release may carry where the scrub leaves it - `publish.scrub.allow` (PROP-003 `CFG-PUBLISH-SCRUB-ALLOW`): the search lets an allowed token through, and the scrub still takes out every group it is in. @status:impl/done

`--no-lfs` publishes a tip that needs no git-lfs: it carries no content git-lfs tracks and no rule that would make git-lfs track anything (`##DECISION-PUBLISH-NO-LFS`). **The git-lfs content of a tree** is every path whose `filter` attribute is `lfs` and whose blob is a git-lfs pointer - a blob of at most 1024 bytes that begins with the line `version https://git-lfs.github.com/spec/v1`. The attribute is resolved from the `.gitattributes` files of that same tree and from nothing else - not from a working directory, not from `$GIT_DIR/info/attributes`, not from the configuration of the machine: `git check-attr --source=<tree> -z --stdin filter` reads the tree itself, with no index to build and nothing checked out, and it runs in a bare repository of the run's scratch, made from an empty template, that reads the objects of the disposable fork through `objects/info/alternates` and so has no `info/attributes`, with `core.attributesFile=/dev/null`, `GIT_ATTR_NOSYSTEM=1` and `core.ignorecase=false`, so that a pattern matches the same way on every machine. The tree and every `.gitattributes` of it are read there first, because `check-attr` answers `unspecified` for a tree it cannot read. **The transformation** of a tree: (1) every path that is git-lfs content is removed; (2) every `.gitattributes` is rewritten by `##PUBLISH-NO-LFS-REWRITE`; (3) a path that has `filter=lfs` but whose blob is not a pointer stays in the tree as the ordinary file it is; (4) the result is checked by `##PUBLISH-NO-LFS-FAIL-CLOSED`. **Where it applies**: with `--squash` - the forms of one commit (`##PUBLISH-FORMS`) - to the release tree, after `--scrub` when that is given and before the commit is written; without `--squash`, after the checks have passed, one more generated commit ends the history. Its tree is the transformation of the tip's tree, and it is written the way the other generated commits are: the author and committer `codkit <codkit@patchset.invalid>`, both dates the committer date of the pin, the subject `codkit: leave out git-lfs content` and the canonical trailers `Codkit-Patchset-Commit` and `Codkit-Upstream-Pin`, without `Codkit-Artifact`; the release tag names this commit. When the transformation leaves the tree as it is - no git-lfs content and no rule - the flag changes nothing: no commit is added, the tree is the same, and the info line `no-lfs: the tree carries no git-lfs content and no git-lfs rule; nothing was left out` says so. The transformation is deterministic, so a repeat against a remote answers `up-to-date`. **The report**: `no-lfs: N git-lfs path(s) left out, M attribute file(s) changed` and one line per changed attribute file; `data.lfs` is `{dropped: [paths], attributes: [paths]}` when the flag is given and null when it is not. Measured on 2026-09-30 on the pin of VS Code 1.135.0 (`08d4889f9ec4a1685d257b9b95de036c8e1ce1e5`): 98 paths, all `extensions/copilot/test/simulation/cache/**/*.sqlite`, and one rule, in `extensions/copilot/.gitattributes`, whose 108 bytes become the 19 bytes `* text=auto eol=lf` and one line feed. The release of 2026-09-25 (`fb7d95ae5610`) made again with `--no-lfs` differs from its tree by exactly those 98 deletions and that one file - 18,509 files against 18,607 - and the owner's check of a tree that needs git-lfs finds neither a pointer nor a rule in it; without `--squash` the history of that patchset commit ends with the one commit `codkit: leave out git-lfs content` on its generated tip `698adbb43cae`. @status:impl/done

How `--no-lfs` rewrites one `.gitattributes` of the tree, byte for byte (`##PUBLISH-NO-LFS` step 2). A line **sets `filter=lfs`** when it is a rule - not blank, not a comment (its first non-blank character is `#`), not a macro definition (`[attr]…`) - and one of the attributes after its pattern is exactly `filter=lfs`; a quoted pattern is read up to its closing quote. Each such line is removed together with the comment lines directly above it: the unbroken run of lines that begin with `#` and end at the removed line, which a blank line or a rule breaks. Then the blank lines at the end of the file are removed, so the file ends with its last non-blank line and the one line ending that line carries. Every other byte of the file stays as it is, its line endings included - CRLF stays CRLF; a line that sets another filter (`filter=x`), or `diff=lfs` without `filter=lfs`, is not touched; a comment that is not directly above a removed line stays; a macro definition and a rule that uses a macro are not rewritten - they are left to `##PUBLISH-NO-LFS-FAIL-CLOSED`. A file with no such line is not touched at all, and a file left without a non-blank line is removed from the tree. A `.gitattributes` that git does not read - a symbolic link - is not touched either. @status:impl/done

The result of `##PUBLISH-NO-LFS` is checked, fail-closed, before the first write to any destination: the attributes of every path of the new tree are resolved again, the same way, and every `.gitattributes` of the new tree is searched for a line that is not a comment and still names `filter=lfs`. A path that still resolves to `filter=lfs` - through a macro, or a rule in a form the rewrite does not remove - stops the publish, and so does such a line that no path of the tree matches today, because it would make git-lfs track the next file it matches: exit 1, `data.status` `lfs-failed`, one `CK-E-CONFIG` error per path naming the path and where its rule comes from - every line that names `filter=lfs` in a `.gitattributes` of the path's directory or of a directory above it, as `<file>:<line>` - and one per such line that no error of a path names already. Nothing is pushed or exported. The way out is the owner's: a plain rule the rewrite removes, a change of the attributes through the patch set, or a release without `--no-lfs`. @status:impl/done

`publishRemoteUrl` may be a local path set in `codkit.local.json`, bare repository or not: the `ls-remote` gate, the lease and the pushes run against it as against a hosted fork. A repository with a working tree takes a push to any branch but the one it has checked out. Measured on 2026-09-24: the e2e fixture publishes into a local bare remote, and a replica of Nimbus published its clean release branch into a bare clone of the upstream repository. A repository that exists already is a remote of this fact; a new one the command creates itself is an export (`##PUBLISH-EXPORT`), and `publishRemoteUrl` is then not read at all. @status:impl/done

`--export-bare <dir>` and `--export-repo <dir>` publish into a **new local repository** the command creates instead of `publishRemoteUrl` (`##DECISION-PUBLISH-EXPORT`): a bare repository, or a repository with a working tree and the release branch checked out. The two exclude each other: both is exit 2 `CK-E-CONFIG` before any gate. With either one `publishRemoteUrl` is neither required nor read, `git ls-remote` is not run, nothing is pushed anywhere and no network is reached (`##PUBLISH-NETWORK-GATE`); `--yes-i-am-publish-bot` stays required and a global `--ci` stays refused with `CK-E-NET-FORBIDDEN`, because an export is the release bot's operation as much as a push, and the wording of both refusals names the export. `<dir>` is absolute or relative to the current directory; it must not exist or must be an empty directory, its parent must exist, and it must not be the patch-set directory or the fork tree or lie inside either of them - compared on their real paths, ignoring case on Windows. Otherwise it is exit 2 `CK-E-CONFIG` after those two gates and before any work, with a hint. The repository is created only after the checks, the squash, the scrub and `--no-lfs` have succeeded: `git init` from an empty template - no hook and no file of any template - in the object format of the disposable fork and with the release branch as its initial branch, so `HEAD` is a symbolic reference to it. The objects go in as one pack that `git pack-objects --revs` writes from the disposable fork straight into the object directory of the repository: exactly the objects the tip reaches - the release tag is a lightweight tag of the tip - stored in the repository itself, with no `objects/info/alternates`, no remote and no path of the disposable fork or of the fork tree anywhere in it. The refs are written without a reflog, so no identity of the machine goes in. After a successful run the repository holds exactly one branch, `refs/heads/<branch>` at the published tip, and the release tag when `--release` is given. Its own configuration carries `core.longpaths=true`, and for `--export-repo` also `core.autocrlf=false` and `core.eol=lf`, so that its working tree is the bytes of the release tree on any machine except where the tree's own attributes demand a line ending: measured on 2026-09-30, the owner's workstation has `core.autocrlf=true` in its global configuration, and a checkout made there by plain git turned every text file to CRLF. For `--export-repo` the working tree is checked out at the tip - with codkit's git, whose attribute files of the machine are switched off as in `##PUBLISH-NO-LFS` - and `git status --porcelain` is empty when plain git of the machine runs it, with the user's global and system configuration. A run that fails leaves no directory behind: what this run created is removed, and a directory that existed empty is left empty. A second run into the same directory is refused, because the directory is no longer empty: there is no lease and no update in place. `data.export` is `{kind: "bare" | "repository", path, lfsObjects}` and null without an export flag; `data.status` is `published`, while `pushedBranch` and `pushedTag` are false and `observedBranch` and `observedTag` null, because nothing was pushed or observed; the closing info line names the repository. Measured on 2026-09-30 on the Nimbus replica: `--squash --scrub --no-lfs --export-repo` wrote a repository with upstream's history - 163,822 commits - in one run of 114 s with its checks; its `.git` holds 1,264 MiB and the repository 1,515 MiB with its working tree, `git fsck --full` passes on it in 44 s, and plain git, whose global configuration on that workstation has `core.autocrlf=true`, sees its working tree clean. @status:impl/done

**git-lfs in an export** (`##PUBLISH-EXPORT`). With `--no-lfs` the repository has no git-lfs objects, no `lfs` section in its configuration and no git-lfs hooks, and `git lfs ls-files` run in it by plain git prints nothing. Without `--no-lfs`, when the tip has git-lfs content (`##PUBLISH-NO-LFS`), the export carries the git-lfs objects **of the tip** - of the tip's tree, not of the history: each object a pointer of the tip names is copied from the lfs storage of the fork tree, `<git-common-dir>/lfs/objects/<oid[0:2]>/<oid[2:4]>/<oid>`, into the export's own - `<dir>/lfs/objects/…` for a bare repository, `<dir>/.git/lfs/objects/…` for one with a working tree - and checked against the size and the sha256 the pointer names. Every object is checked in the fork tree before the repository is created: an object the fork tree does not have, one that does not match its pointer, and a pointer that names no sha256 object are exit 2 `CK-E-LFS` naming the paths and the object ids, with the hint to fetch them into the fork tree (`git -C <fork tree> lfs fetch origin <pin.sha>` - a bare `git lfs fetch` fetches for the tree's HEAD, which need not be the pin); Codkit does not reach the network for them. For `--export-repo`, when git-lfs is installed, the repository's own configuration carries the lfs filters that `git lfs install --local --skip-repo` writes, the checkout smudges from the repository's own storage, and the working tree holds the content of those files, so that plain git sees the tree clean; git-lfs then adds its hooks and an `lfs` section to that configuration by itself. The checkout names the repository's own hooks directory as `core.hooksPath`: it runs no hook, and git-lfs, which installs its hooks where `core.hooksPath` points, reads the `/dev/null` of codkit's isolated git (PROP-002 `GIT-ENV-ISOLATION`) as a directory of the working tree on Windows - measured on 2026-09-30 with git-lfs 3.7.1, it wrote its four hooks into an untracked `dev/null/` of the export's working tree. When git-lfs is not installed, the objects are still carried, the working tree holds the pointer files, and a warning says so. The older commits of upstream may reference git-lfs objects too; they are not carried, so a checkout of an older commit of an export with history needs them from elsewhere. `data.export.lfsObjects` is the number of objects carried. A push to `publishRemoteUrl` - no export flag - stays as it was: git objects only. Measured on 2026-09-30 on the Nimbus replica: a bare export of one commit carried the 98 objects of the tip of 1.135.0, each matching its pointer, in 317.7 MiB; a plain `git clone` of it checked out the content of all 98 files, and so did the export of the generated history with a working tree, which plain git sees clean. @status:impl/done

`publish` takes the inputs of the published commit's `codkit.json` from their pinned commits, found where `codkit.local.json` of this machine places them (PROP-003 `LOCAL-CONFIG-RULE`), through the checks of `ci` (`##CI-INPUTS`): the history ends with one commit per input (`##INPUTS-GENERATED`), so without `--squash` each input is one more commit on top of the per-artifact history, carrying `Codkit-Input: <name>@<commit>` besides the canonical trailers, and with `--squash` its files are part of the one commit, which carries no trailer. The files of an input are delivered files of `##PUBLISH-SCRUB` - the pin does not carry them - so the scrub, `publish.exclude` and the search of `##PUBLISH-SCRUB-FAIL-CLOSED` cover them as they cover any file the patch set adds. Every refusal of an input - a ref its repository lacks, `##INPUTS-BUILD`, `##INPUTS-OUTPUT`, `##INPUTS-PLACEMENT` - is exit 2 `CK-E-CONFIG` before the first remote write. The result names each input with its commit and the number of files the pushed tree carries at its `to` - `input <name>: <commit12> -> <to>: N file(s)` - and `data.inputs` is `[{name, commit, to, files}]`. Measured on 2026-09-24 on the Nimbus replica: an input the documentation repository builds with `node tools/docbuild/cli.mjs build --no-diagrams` delivered 126 files at `documentation`, `documentation/doc.yaml` among them; `publish --squash --scrub` took 73 s, changed none of the 126 files and found no leftover in them, and a repeat answered `up-to-date` with the same tip - that build is deterministic. @status:impl/done

**Decision:** a release commit without a parent is `--orphan`, a modifier of `--squash`, and not a form with a flag of its own.

**Why:** the one commit for everything is the squashed commit of `##PUBLISH-SQUASH` with its parent left out - the same tree, author, message and date, the same `--scrub` and `--no-lfs`; only the parent differs, and a modifier keeps one set of rules for both commits and one place where they differ. They are two different deliveries: on 2026-09-29 and 2026-09-30 the release commit was written again by hand, once without a parent and once on the pin, and the owner once received the commit without any history where he expected upstream's history under it - so each is asked for by name, and `--squash` alone keeps meaning the commit on the pin.

**Considered and rejected:**
- `--orphan` alone implying `--squash` - it would squash a history nobody asked to squash, and a squashed commit needs `--author` and `--message-file`, which the run would then refuse for a flag it was never given;
- a value of `--squash` (`--squash orphan`) - `--squash` is a boolean flag of `save` and `sync` as well, and one spelling cannot take a value on one command and none on the others;
- a separate flag such as `--single-commit` - two flags for one commit whose rules must stay the same.

**When to revisit:** when a release needs a squashed commit on another parent than the pin or none - observed as a request for a base other than `pin.sha`. @status:impl/done

**Decision:** `--no-lfs` removes the content git-lfs tracks and the rules that make it track anything, and it exists only as a flag given on the run - the one exception to `##PUBLISH-EXCLUDE`, which otherwise never lets a release lose upstream's bytes.

**Why:** the owner's order of 2026-09-30: the product source goes to a CI Git server that has no git-lfs and to an isolated network that receives an archive, and on 2026-09-29 and 2026-09-30 the git-lfs content was removed from the release tree by hand, with its rule, twice. On VS Code 1.135.0 that content is 98 paths, all SQLite fixtures of the tests of one extension (`extensions/copilot/test/simulation/cache/**/*.sqlite`), whose pointers name 272,367,616 bytes - measured on 2026-09-30, of 277,359,693 bytes in the 584 objects of the fork tree's git-lfs storage - and the product never ships them; the rule is one line in one file.

**Considered and rejected:**
- turning each pointer into an ordinary git blob of its content - the release would stay complete, but carry about 272 MB of test fixtures the product never ships into every clone and every archive, against 98 removed paths;
- a value in `codkit.json` or `codkit.local.json` - the owner's order is that every choice is a flag of the command; a configuration value would remove upstream bytes from every later release without anybody asking for it on the run;
- `publish.exclude` for the pointers - it refuses a path of the pin on purpose, and that refusal stays as it is.

**When to revisit:** when a product ships a file that git-lfs tracks - observed as a path of `data.lfs.dropped` that the product build or the product itself needs, or as a build of the delivered source that fails after `--no-lfs`; such paths are then carried as ordinary blobs instead. @status:impl/done

**Decision:** an export is a new repository `publish` creates itself - bare, or with a working tree - holding the objects of the tip and nothing else; a directory that exists and is not empty is refused, and the git-lfs objects it carries are those of the tip.

**Why:** on 2026-09-29 and 2026-09-30 a self-contained repository with a working tree was made by hand out of the bare remote of a release (`git init`, `git fetch`, `git reset`, `gc`), and once the owner was pointed at a bare repository where he needed a real one. A repository the command creates from nothing carries nothing it did not put there - no remote, no alternates, no path of the machine, no reflog - so it can be packed and handed on as it is. The older git-lfs objects are upstream's archive, not the release: of the 584 objects in the git-lfs storage of the VS Code fork tree the tip of 1.135.0 names 98 (measured on 2026-09-30).

**Considered and rejected:**
- a push into an existing local repository - that is `publishRemoteUrl` already (`##PUBLISH-LOCAL-REMOTE`); what such a repository holds besides the release is not the command's to know, and one with a working tree refuses a push to the branch it has checked out;
- an update of an export in place, with a lease - an export is a delivery made once; a second run into the same directory would mix two releases in one repository;
- carrying the git-lfs objects of the whole history - the release is its tip, and a contour that needs an older commit's objects fetches them from upstream.

**When to revisit:** when a contour needs the git-lfs objects of older commits, or an export updated in place - observed as a request after a delivery, or as an export that is copied over by hand once more. @status:impl/done
19. codkit hooks install|check
